options.title: The Doctor Who Was Mocked For Washing Hands
options.description: In 1847, Ignaz Semmelweis introduced chlorine handwashing at Vienna General Hospital, drastically reducing maternal mortality. Sources: CDC History of Handwashing, World Health Organization historical archives.
script_lines: In 1847, a Hungarian doctor forced his entire medical team to soak their hands in harsh bleach before touching patients.
Ignaz Semmelweis realized mothers delivered by doctors died at three times the rate of those delivered by midwives.
His chief physician mocked him, scoffing, 'Gentlemen are clean; disease lives in bad air, not hands!'
Semmelweis stayed stubborn, standing directly by the door with a tub of chlorinated lime water.
At first, doctors complained about ruined skin and deliberately skipped the soak whenever he looked away.
But when washing became mandatory, maternal mortality in his ward dropped from eighteen percent down to less than two.
Particles from the morgue were hitching rides on dry skin, acting like invisible wet paint passed from doctor to patient.
It took decades for science to catch up, all because one man forced doctors to wash their hands.

options.title: The First Controlled Clinical Trial at Sea
options.description: In 1747, James Lind conducted one of the first controlled clinical trials in history aboard HMS Salisbury to cure scurvy. Sources: Royal Navy Medical Service Records, James Lind's 'A Treatise of the Scurvy' (1753).
script_lines: In 1747, a ship's surgeon fed two scurvy-ridden sailors sour lemons while giving others sulfuric acid and seawater.
James Lind was trapped on HMS Salisbury, where a mysterious disease was rotting sailors from the inside out.
Senior physicians laughed at his experiment, sneering, 'Citrus is an expensive snack, not real medicine!'
Lind ignored them, carefully dividing twelve sick men into six pairs to test six different remedies.
For days, the men drinking vinegar and saltwater only grew weaker, while skeptics called the test a waste of supplies.
But on day six, the two lemon-eaters suddenly stood up, fully recovered, and began nursing the other ten men.
The missing vitamin C was causing their cellular walls to break down like mortar crumbling out of a brick chimney.
Proving that a simple piece of fruit could defend an entire empire at sea.

options.title: The Messy Workbench That Saved Millions
options.description: In 1928, Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin by accident after leaving a Petri dish exposed to mold. Sources: Nobel Prize Archives, St. Mary's Hospital Historical Records.
script_lines: In 1928, a messy Scottish doctor returned from vacation and refused to wash a moldy dish of bacteria.
Alexander Fleming was sorting through cluttered glass culture plates in his dusty London laboratory.
His lab assistant scoffed, saying, 'Throw that ruined trash away so we can start over.'
Fleming paused, staring closely at a strange blue fuzzy spot, and replied, 'That's funny.'
Mold contaminants were a daily headache for researchers, usually meaning weeks of wasted effort.
But around this specific mold blob, thousands of staph bacteria had completely dissolved into clear liquid.
The mold was secreting penicillin, a molecule that punctures bacterial walls like needles popping tiny water balloons.
Modern medicine was born simply because a doctor refused to wash his dirty dish.
